name: Followers of Set: Faith, Schism, and the Ruins of Tanis (Dark Ages)

pages.name: The Ceremony of Opening the Door

text.content:
Source: Libellus Sanguinis III: Wolves at the Door, Book Three ("Serpents").

Unlike other Cainites, a Follower of Set cannot simply be chosen; the god's essence must be asked for, never offered, and sharing it with one who is unworthy is among the gravest offenses a Setite can commit. Nearly all of Set's children begin as victims of another Setite's patient, often decades-long seduction. Most mortals lured toward the darkness recoil in horror; some simply surrender to their appetites and are of no further use. A rare few neither break nor bend, finding purpose in the carnal truths the Setite reveals to them, and it is only these who are deemed worthy to become vessels of the god.

The Embrace itself is preceded by a rite called the Ceremony of Opening the Door, performed only on the night of the new moon. The supplicant is bathed and anointed with scented oil at the sire's house, then brought naked before an effigy of Set. The sire presents a curved knife to the god's image and recites an invocation in the language of ancient Egypt, then passes the knife to the supplicant, who kneels, opens his own veins, and lets his blood wash over the god's face while confessing aloud his many appetites and depravities, proving himself a fitting vessel. As the supplicant's life ebbs, the sire comes forward and lets him drink the dark river of vitae in his own veins — and the supplicant's akh is said to fly on falcon's wings into Du'at as his body becomes a house of the god.

pages.name: Setite Cosmology: Ra, Osiris, and the Two Worlds

text.content:
Source: Libellus Sanguinis III: Wolves at the Door, Book Three ("Serpents").

The @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.ssX4b2JFXF2uegC3]{Followers of Set} do not consider themselves vampires akin to the Cainites of Europe; they see the European "Children of Caine" as descendants or servants of evil spirits loosed when Ra usurped the afterlife (Du'at) from its rightful balance, or Maat. In the Setite telling, the chieftain Ra and his grandson Osiris conspired to bind humanity in the artificial chains of law and shame, denying mankind the fierce, appetite-driven existence the gods intended. Set alone saw the deception, and after his brother Ra exiled him to die in the desert, Set drank of a hidden spring — the dark river between worlds — and became the first of the undying, straddling life and death. Learning the truth, Set trapped Osiris in a sarcophagus and cast him into the Nile, then shared his blood with Egypt's wisest priests and scholars so that they, too, might perceive the truth and spread it: the first Followers of Set.

Roughly a millennium ago, Set spoke for seven nights running to all his childer down to the sixth generation in a great foretelling now called the Prophecies of Set, then vanished from his sarcophagus at Tanis; none know when or whether he will return. Some 300 prophecies are attributed to him, of which perhaps a third are believed fulfilled either by chance or the deliberate labor of Setite cabals. No single Setite knows them all; each Hierophant elder passes fragments to his childer as a sacred duty, though in recent decades some elders have begun hoarding their knowledge to bolster their own standing, straining the loyalty of younger generations.

Source: Libellus Sanguinis III: Wolves at the Door, Book Three ("Serpents").

After the drowning of Tanis (destroyed by storm, flood, and a vengeful Lupine assault after Set's disappearance left the city's defenders bereft of his power), the eldest surviving Setites — those who had drunk directly from the god and attended him at Tanis — assumed leadership of the clan in his absence. Called the Hierophants, there are seven of them today (six others remain entombed beneath the drowned city). The greatest is Nakhthorheb, the First Son, said to share Set's own tribe and blood; he rules the Hierophants through will and the implicit threat of the god's wrath, regarding all non-Egyptians as little better than animals and all Cainites as enemies. Second in influence is Seterpenre (also rendered Setepenre), Lord of Tinnis and a former sorcerer, who is more tolerant of outsiders and orchestrated an early (and costly, in Nakhthorheb's eyes) Setite alliance with the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.jaYCq9rVOh0I9NCN]{Tremere}. The third, Maatkare, said to have been Set's own concubine, builds consensus among the elders and holds influence rivaling the other two, though her motives remain her own.

Not every surviving Setite accepted the Hierophants' authority. Suspecting that one of the surviving elders had betrayed Tanis to the Lupines, many descendants of the drowned city held instead to loyalty toward one's immediate sire and childer alone. Pushed by the Hierophants first into Palestine and later into Constantinople, these Setites organized into the Decadents (called the Children of Judas in Christian lands), a faction now concentrated in the corrupt remnants of the Byzantine Empire and more interested in corruption for its own sake than in restoring Egypt's glory. Their leader, a Nubian tribesman named Khay'tall, denies Nakhthorheb's authority outright and promotes evil itself as the true object of worship rather than a mere tool of Set. His childe Sarrasine outwardly agrees while quietly gathering allies to one day supplant him, and has broken with tradition by sharing Set's blood with unworthy souls, including the exiled French knight Jules Talbot, an infernalist now serving as Sarrasine's lieutenant in Constantinople's Latin Quarter, driven by pure material ambition rather than religious devotion. A separate creation of Khay'tall, the corrupted Bishop Benedict Alphonso, has fused the worship of Set with worship of his own debased Lucifer and is spreading this double heresy across Europe through his own pupils.

The Third Crusade has driven the Hierophants to mandate that @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.ssX4b2JFXF2uegC3]{Followers of Set} push outward beyond Egypt's borders, but the resulting younger generations, raised with little connection to Egypt, increasingly find common cause with the Decadents rather than their own elders — a growing rift that threatens the clan with outright schism.

pages.name: Tanis, Tinnis, and the Setite Homeland

text.content:
Source: Libellus Sanguinis III: Wolves at the Door, Book Three ("Serpents").

Tanis was the ancient city where Setite elders gathered in the Ptolemaic era to receive the god's wisdom and, later, the terrible seven nights of the Prophecies of Set. After the god's disappearance, Roman raids weakened the city's mortal infrastructure, and a great storm brought a Lupine assault the weakened Setites could not repel; the flooding of Lake Manzala afterward drowned the city's vaults and tunnels, entombing many elders and treasures beneath the water and sand. Some Setites still claim to hear the drowned elders calling out to their descendants, summoning them back into the deep.

The surviving mortal population fled to found Tinnis, a sister city on an island in Lake Manzala, now a prosperous textile-trading center and the only city in Egypt ruled openly by a Setite prince: the Hierophant elder Setepenre, who has welcomed Greek-born @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.ZFYurbvAHfaRguYI]{Brujah}, Cappadocian, and @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador} scholars to study the ruins of Tanis under his supervision while turning back two separate @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.jaYCq9rVOh0I9NCN]{Tremere}-sponsored expeditions.

At the oasis of Siwa, where Alexander the Great's priests once confirmed his belief in his own divinity, the Hierophant elder Tenermentu maintains a temple of prophecy where mortals and Cainites alike come seeking to know their destinies — destinies the Setite oracle shapes carefully around each supplicant's hidden desires.
